6.1.crux: Combustion is a chemical reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen and gives off heat and often light; it only starts once the substance is heated to its ignition temperature.

cards.title: What burns?

cols.head: Combustible
cells: Paper, wood, kerosene, charcoal, LPG, matchstick

say: A substance that reacts with oxygen and gives off heat is combustible.
This reaction is called combustion.

cards.title: Fire needs air

steps.text: A candle burns well in open air
Cover it with a glass jar: the flame flickers
When the oxygen inside is used up, the flame goes out

say: Oxygen in the air is needed for combustion.
That's why we cover a burning cloth with a blanket to put out the fire.

cards.title: Ignition temperature
say: The lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire is its ignition temperature.
A paper cup with water in it won't burn over a flame: the water keeps the paper below its ignition temperature.

cards.title: Easy to catch fire
say: Substances with a very low ignition temperature are called inflammable.
They catch fire easily, so they must be stored with great care.

cards.title: How a match lights

steps.text: The side of the box has powdered glass and red phosphorus
Rubbing the match head on it makes heat
A little red phosphorus turns into white phosphorus, which lights the match head

say: The match head has antimony trisulphide and potassium chlorate.
Old matches used poisonous white phosphorus and were dangerous.

crux_points: Combustion is a reaction with oxygen that gives off heat (and often light).
A substance burns only after reaching its ignition temperature.
Inflammable substances like petrol and LPG have very low ignition temperatures.

quiz.q: A candle under a glass jar goes out because…
options: The oxygen inside gets used up
quiz.why: Combustion needs oxygen; once it's used up, the flame dies.

quiz.q: The lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire is its…
quiz.why: Below its ignition temperature, a substance won't catch fire.

6.2.crux: Fire needs fuel, air and heat; a fire extinguisher works by taking away one or more of these.

cards.title: The fire triangle
say: Take away any one side of the triangle and the fire goes out.

cards.title: Water: cools and covers

steps.text: Water cools the burning material below its ignition temperature
Steam from the water surrounds the fire and cuts off air
The fire stops

say: Water is the most common fire extinguisher. It works best on wood and paper.

cards.title: When NOT to use water

cols.head: Electrical fire
cells: The person can get a shock

cols.head: Oil or petrol fire
cells: Oil floats on top and keeps burning

say: Never throw water on burning oil or on electrical equipment.

cards.title: Carbon dioxide: the best choice

items.sub: Covers the fire like a blanket
The fire is starved of air

say: Carbon dioxide is best for fires in electrical equipment and in petrol or oil.
It is stored as a liquid at high pressure in cylinders. Baking soda near a fire also gives off carbon dioxide.

crux_points: Fire needs fuel, air (oxygen) and heat.
Water cools the fire and cuts off air, but must not be used on electrical or oil fires.
Carbon dioxide blankets the fire and is safe for electrical and oil fires.

quiz.q: What is marked '?' in the fire triangle?
quiz.why: The three sides of the fire triangle are fuel, heat and air (oxygen).

quiz.q: Why shouldn't you pour water on burning oil?
options: Oil floats on water and keeps burning
quiz.why: Oil is lighter than water, so it floats on top and keeps burning.

quiz.q: Which extinguisher is best for a fire in a computer?
quiz.why: Carbon dioxide doesn't conduct electricity and doesn't damage equipment.

6.3.crux: Combustion can be rapid (gas on a stove), spontaneous (catches fire by itself) or an explosion (sudden, with a loud sound).

cards.title: Three types of combustion

cols.head: Rapid
cells: Burns fast, giving heat and light

cols.head: Spontaneous
cells: Bursts into flame without any visible cause
Phosphorus at room temperature; coal dust in mines

cols.head: Explosion
cells: Sudden reaction with heat, light, sound and lots of gas

say: Not every fire starts the same way.

cards.title: Forest fires

items.sub: Can heat dry leaves enough to burn
Can strike and set trees alight
Most forest fires are started by people

say: Forest fires can start by themselves in very hot, dry weather.
But most are caused by human carelessness.

cards.title: Explosions

steps.text: A cracker is lit
It reacts suddenly, making lots of gas, heat, light and sound
Explosions can also happen when crackers are pressed hard

say: Handle crackers only under adult supervision.

crux_points: Rapid combustion: burns quickly with heat and light (LPG).
Spontaneous combustion: catches fire by itself (phosphorus).
Explosion: sudden reaction with heat, light, sound and gas (crackers).

quiz.q: Phosphorus catches fire in air at room temperature. This is…
quiz.why: It burns by itself without being lit: spontaneous combustion.

quiz.q: A firecracker going off is an example of…
quiz.why: An explosion is a sudden reaction giving heat, light, sound and gas.

6.4.crux: Substances that turn into vapour when they burn, like wax and kerosene, burn with a flame; charcoal just glows.

cards.title: Flame or glow?
say: Some things burn with a flame, others just glow red-hot.

cards.title: Why wax makes a flame

steps.text: Heat melts the wax near the wick
Liquid wax rises up the wick
The wax turns into vapour
The vapour burns, giving a flame

say: Only substances that vaporise while burning give a flame.
Charcoal doesn't vaporise, so it only glows.

cards.title: More things that make flames

items.sub: Kerosene rises up the wick and vaporises
Turns to vapour easily, so it flames
Already a gas, so it burns with a flame

say: Anything that is a gas, or becomes a vapour as it burns, gives a flame.

crux_points: A flame forms when a substance vaporises as it burns.
Wax and kerosene burn with flames; charcoal only glows.
In a candle, molten wax rises up the wick and vaporises.

quiz.q: Why does charcoal glow without a flame?
options: It doesn't vaporise when it burns
quiz.why: Only substances that vaporise during burning give a flame.

quiz.q: In a candle, what actually burns in the flame?
quiz.why: Molten wax rises up the wick, turns into vapour, and the vapour burns.

6.5.crux: A candle flame has three zones: a dark inner zone of unburnt wax vapour, a bright yellow middle zone and a hot blue outer zone.

cards.title: Three zones

labels.name: Innermost zone
labels.note: Dark: unburnt wax vapour, least hot

say: Look closely at a candle flame: it isn't all the same colour.
cards.remember: Dark inside, yellow middle, blue outside (hottest).

cards.title: Compare the zones
say: The outer zone gets the most air, so burning there is complete.

cards.title: Proofs and uses

items.sub: Gets a black ring of unburnt carbon (soot)
Blow the hottest outer zone onto gold and silver to melt them

say: The black soot shows that carbon in the middle zone is not fully burnt.

crux_points: Innermost zone: dark, unburnt vapour, least hot.
Middle zone: yellow and bright, partial combustion.
Outermost zone: blue, complete combustion, the hottest.

quiz.why: The blue outer zone has complete combustion and is the hottest part.

quiz.q: Which zone of the flame gives the most light?
quiz.why: The middle zone is luminous: glowing carbon particles give the yellow light.

6.6.crux: A fuel burns to give heat; a good fuel is cheap, easy to get, burns at a steady rate, gives lots of heat and leaves little waste.

cards.title: Fuels in three states
say: Anything that burns to give us useful heat is a fuel.

cards.title: A good fuel is…

items.text: Burns easily at a moderate rate

say: No fuel is perfect (ideal).
We choose the fuel that best fits the job.
cards.remember: There is no ideal fuel; we pick the best one for each use.

cards.title: Choosing a cooking fuel
say: That's why many homes have switched from wood to LPG for cooking.
Smoke from wood fires harms the lungs.

crux_points: A fuel burns to give useful heat.
Fuels can be solid, liquid or gas.
A good fuel is cheap, available, burns steadily, gives lots of heat and leaves little residue.

quiz.q: Which of these is a gaseous fuel?
quiz.why: LPG (liquefied petroleum gas) burns as a gas.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a feature of a good fuel?
options: Leaves lots of smoke and ash
quiz.why: A good fuel leaves little or no harmful residue.

6.7.crux: Calorific value is the heat a fuel gives when 1 kg burns completely; burning fuels also releases harmful gases and soot.

cards.title: Calorific values (kJ per kg)
say: Calorific value tells us how much heat 1 kg of a fuel gives on burning completely.
It is measured in kilojoules per kilogram (kJ/kg).
cards.remember: Higher calorific value = more heat from the same amount of fuel.

cards.title: Harm from burning fuels
say: Never sleep in a closed room with a coal fire burning: carbon monoxide can kill.

cards.title: Global warming

steps.text: Burning fuels adds extra carbon dioxide to the air
The Earth's average temperature rises
Polar ice and glaciers melt
Sea level rises and low coastal areas flood

say: Using cleaner fuels like CNG and saving energy reduces this harm.

cards.title: Acid rain
say: Acid rain harms crops, buildings and soil.

crux_points: Calorific value = heat from burning 1 kg of fuel completely (kJ/kg).
Hydrogen has the highest calorific value; cow dung cakes are among the lowest.
Burning fuels releases soot, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide (global warming) and gases that cause acid rain.

quiz.q: Which fuel has the highest calorific value?
quiz.why: Hydrogen gives about 150,000 kJ/kg, far more than other fuels.

quiz.q: Why is it dangerous to sleep in a closed room with a coal fire?
quiz.why: Incomplete burning makes carbon monoxide, a deadly poisonous gas.
